title: Meet the FT Law 50: shaping the future
pub: Financial Times — Special Report, FT Legal Outlook (FT Innovative Lawyers programme, with research partner RSGI)
author: Financial Times

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the proposition that in-house legal departments can become the principal drivers and beneficiaries of AI-enabled delivery redesign. It provides examples of departments embedding AI, developing bespoke legal products and potentially bypassing law firms that fail to adapt, while offering illustrative initiatives rather than measured evidence of realised gains.
qs: He argues that some in-house teams are already building AI-powered legal systems, and law firms that fail to engage with the technology risk being “designed around” by their own clients.

Gitte Groenewold-Wong Head of group legal, Prosus  As befits a senior lawyer at a technology investment business, Gitte Groenewold-Wong is pushing her team of lawyers to use AI to custom-build their own legal products.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s restructuring thesis by identifying AI-driven investment, new firm models, operational upheaval and changes to lawyer training. Its reference to a “potentially existential” threat is framed as a possibility rather than evidence of wholesale elimination, and it provides no employment data or detailed analysis showing that junior pipelines face the sharpest risk.
qs: It faces the potentially existential threat of AI, which has led to an explosion of investment into the legal technology sector ($4.28bn in 2025, according to market intelligence platform Legaltech Hub), and the emergence of new law firm business models, including so-called AI-native firms,  which have put the tech at their core from the outset.

Managing partners and corporate general counsel must contend with upheavals to the way they  work, to their relationships with each other, and to their strategies for training the next generation of lawyers.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that legal AI is progressing beyond isolated task efficiency toward operating-model and client-relationship change. It also reinforces buyer-led bargaining pressure by showing an in-house legal department evaluating outside counsel’s AI adoption, while its reported benefits remain customer-reported rather than independently measured.
qs: But now the challenge is to use AI not simply as a research assistant or chatbot, but to help restructure the relationship with clients.

In addition to creating the role of a dedicated chief AI and transformation officer role within Salesforce’s legal department, he also evaluates outside counsel on adoption of the technology as a criterion for retention.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source corroborates Harvey’s substantial commercial traction through user growth and valuation, while offering no evidence that these metrics establish legal performance or durable defensibility. Its discussion of training and usage tracking also aligns with the cluster’s view that implementation matters beyond purchasing.
qs: After Harvey gained early access to OpenAI’s GPT-4 large language model, which showed potential for greater legal reasoning ability than its predecessor, it has grown to serve more than 100,000 legal professionals worldwide.
Its March funding round valued it at $11bn.

kp.k: AI investment accompanies potentially existential industry change
kp.d: The report frames AI as a potentially existential threat to elite commercial law and links it to legal-technology investment of $4.28bn in 2025, attributed to Legaltech Hub, and the emergence of AI-native firms. It identifies changes to working methods, firm–client relationships and lawyer training, rather than presenting measured evidence of industry-wide displacement.
qs: These are unsettling times for the global legal industry, and particularly for the elite commercial segment covered by the FT’s Innovative Lawyers programme.

It faces the potentially existential threat of AI, which has led to an explosion of investment into the legal technology sector ($4.28bn in 2025, according to market intelligence platform Legaltech Hub), and the emergence of new law firm business models, including so-called AI-native firms,

kp.k: In-house automation may displace outside counsel assignments
kp.d: The FT argues that digital systems may affect in-house lawyers more than private practitioners: routine work can be automated and some work previously outsourced can remain inside corporate departments. More time for senior lawyers to provide strategic advice is explicitly presented as a promise, not a demonstrated outcome.
qs: The increasing use of new digital systems in business is arguably affecting lawyers who are working  in-house more than those in private practice.

AI means that more labour-intensive routine tasks can now be automated; work that would once have required engaging outside counsel can be done in-house; and the promise is that there will be  more time for senior lawyers to advise on strategic business matters.

kp.k: Corporate legal departments deploy numerous AI agents
kp.d: The report describes operational adoption at CrowdStrike, where Cathleen Anderson's team of more than 80 has received training and deployed more than 100 legal AI agents, alongside her company-wide AI mandate. At Prosus, Gitte Groenewold-Wong's team has created nearly 300 agents; she also used Claude Code to build a regulatory tracker. These are deployment examples, without quantified productivity or quality evaluations.
qs: Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike was among the first businesses to give its chief legal officer a company-wide mandate to champion AI adoption beyond the in-house legal team.
Cathleen Anderson leads a team of more than 80, which has been trained in the technology and now has more than 100 AI agents for legal work deployed.

Her team at Dutch company Prosus has created nearly 300 AI agents offering reductions in  labour-intensive tasks, while Groenewold-Wong herself recently used the AI coding agent Claude Code to build a regulatory tracker.

kp.k: Buyers increasingly shape providers' AI adoption
kp.d: Salesforce chief legal officer Sabastian Niles evaluates outside counsel's technology adoption when deciding retention and has created a dedicated legal-department AI and transformation leadership role. Separately, Cox Media Group general counsel Eric D. Greenberg argues that clients building their own AI systems could bypass firms that fail to engage. The latter is an attributed competitive warning, not an established market-wide finding.
qs: In addition to creating the role of a dedicated chief AI and transformation officer role within Salesforce’s legal department, he also evaluates outside counsel on adoption of the technology as a criterion for retention.
He argues that some in-house teams are already building AI-powered legal systems, and law firms that fail to engage with the technology risk being “designed around” by their own clients.

kp.k: AI becomes infrastructure for corporate legal service delivery
kp.d: At Coherent, Rob Beard has embedded a purpose-built platform across the legal function to facilitate company-wide legal intelligence. National Grid's Justine Campbell is making AI central to modernising service delivery across approximately 450 employees handling legal, compliance, risk and safety, including sharing practices internally and with external firms.
qs: An early adopter of pioneering AI software designed for in-house legal teams, Beard has embedded a purpose-built AI platform across Coherent’s legal function, making it easier to gather company-  wide legal intelligence.

Justine Campbell leads one of Europe’s largest corporate in-house legal departments, with about 450 employees handling legal, compliance, risk and safety for the energy utility, which operates in the UK and US.
Initiatives include efforts to disseminate best practice in legal tech use, both within the legal team and in its collaborations with outside law firms.

kp.k: Initial adoption must progress toward client-relationship redesign
kp.d: The FT reports rapid uptake and customer-reported time savings and workplace satisfaction from Harvey and Legora. Its proposed next challenge is to move beyond research-assistant and chatbot use toward restructuring client relationships. The report supplies no customer sample, quantified gains or independent assessment for these benefit claims.
qs: Early take-up has been swift by law firms and  companies, and customers of the platforms developed by US start-up Harvey and its European rival Legora typically report rapid gains in time savings and workplace satisfaction.
But now the challenge is to use AI not simply as a research assistant or chatbot, but to help restructure the relationship with clients.

kp.k: AI-first workflows prompt billing and remuneration reconsideration
kp.d: Ashurst Advance leader Hilary Goodier is tracking client buying behaviour and AI capabilities while pursuing billing models reflecting both technology and human skills. The firm increasingly organises people and processes around AI. MinterEllison's Virginia Briggs is planning possible pricing and remuneration changes; the report does not claim these changes have already occurred.
qs: Goodier has led efforts to track how clients now buy legal services and the tasks AI can undertake, and to move to billing models that take into account both the technology and the human skills involved.
In a shift in strategy, Ashurst’s approach is increasingly to start with AI and organise  processes and people around the tech.
She is also  already planning for potential changes to pricing of services and the effects on lawyers’ remuneration.

kp.k: Training combines incentives, usage tracking and psychological support
kp.d: The report describes MinterEllison's training rewards through Mintcoin, partner training and an Applied Innovation team established in 2024. Mallesons certifies AI proficiency and tracks use following platform rollout. ALSP Factor's Sensemaker Academy, developed with King's College London's law school, responds to lawyers' anxiety about AI; Positive Group addresses psychological aspects of adoption. These are implementation approaches, not demonstrated comparative training outcomes.
qs: Mintcoin, an internal digital currency used to reward staff who undertake AI training
She even added an “AI belt” as the sixth in the firm’s suite of martial arts-style “legal transformation belts”, which certify proficiency.
Keen to make sure that training is effective, she developed a system to track how lawyers put to use the legal AI platform it rolled out last year.
After co-founding alternative services provider Factor in 2019, Chris DeConti identified widespread anxiety about using AI as a big challenge facing the legal profession.
A recent focus is guiding law firms through psychological aspects of adopting AI.

kp.k: Legal education expands AI skills and research capacity
kp.d: Examples span professional and academic formation: ACC offers AI training and guidance to approximately 48,000 members; Wei Chen's Atticus Project builds open-source legal AI datasets and supports skills development; Brian Tang incorporates generative AI into legal education. Cyril Shroff endowed an AI, law and regulation centre with $1.8mn, while his firm piloted technology with 380 lawyers before platform selection.
qs: The potential of AI is a key preoccupation, and the ACC’s 48,000 or so  members can access training and guidance via the organisation’s Center of Excellence in the technology.
This non-profit organisation builds open-source datasets for legal AI and helps lawyers at all levels to sharpen their skills in the technology.
Brian Tang is one of the world’s first law school educators to incorporate generative AI into the curriculum.
The Cyril Shroff Centre for Artificial Intelligence, Law and Regulation, based at the Jindal Global Law School near Delhi, has been endowed with $1.8mn from Shroff.
He is also actively involved in the embrace of AI by his own firm, which recently ran a pilot scheme  involving 380 lawyers before choosing its legal tech platform.

kp.k: Junior task substitution could enable higher-value work
kp.d: Harvey co-founder Gabe Pereyra argues that AI will absorb some junior lawyers' tasks while potentially enabling them to move into higher-value work. The report attributes this position to him and provides no measured employment, staffing-leverage or career-development outcomes.
qs: A thoughtful commentator on AI, Pereyra has argued that while AI will absorb some tasks currently undertaken by junior lawyers, it can also propel them into higher-value work.

kp.k: Vendors attract capital and scale internationally
kp.d: The report places Harvey at more than 100,000 legal-professional users and an $11bn valuation following its March funding round; Legora serves more than 50 markets and reached a $5.6bn valuation after its latest 2026 fundraising. The LegalTech Fund's second fund closed at $110mn in November 2025, compared with its initial $28.5mn vehicle, and its portfolio exceeds 80 companies. These figures describe investment and reach rather than verified legal performance.
qs: it has grown to serve more than 100,000 legal professionals worldwide. Its March funding round valued it at $11bn.

The three-year-old legal AI start-up co-founded by Swedish entrepreneur Max Junestrand is valued at $5.6bn following its latest 2026 fundraising, the highest valuation for a European legal tech company.
now serves clients in more than 50 markets.
TLTF’s second fund closed at $110mn in November 2025, nearly four times the size of the inaugural $28.5mn vehicle.
TLTF now has a portfolio of more than 80 companies

kp.k: Research data and practice management converge
kp.d: Clio, reported to serve more than 400,000 legal professionals, acquired vLex for $1bn in November 2025 alongside a $500mn funding round valuing Clio at $5bn. The acquisition supplied access to more than 1bn legal documents from more than 100 countries. Damien Riehl oversees integration of case-law data with Clio's management software, illustrating the combination of legal information and workflow products.
qs: it now serves more than 400,000 legal professionals.
In November 2025, Clio bought legal research platform vLex for $1bn, alongside a $500mn funding round that valued the company at $5bn.
The transaction secured Clio’s access to vLex’s archive of more than 1bn legal documents drawn from court decisions, governments and  publishers in more than 100 countries.
he oversees the integration of a vast  case-law database with its own law firm management software.

kp.k: Law firms become legal technology developers
kp.d: Freshfields' April partnership with Anthropic involves developing specialist tools potentially sold to other firms, contrasting with competitors' off-the-shelf platform partnerships. Hogan Lovells' Eltemate venture, launched in 2023, consolidates client technology offerings and develops proprietary regulatory-update and task-automation tools. Anthropic also launched Claude for Legal in May following February legal plug-ins.
qs: the UK-based “magic circle” law firm agreed a pioneering deal in April with US-based AI company Anthropic to develop specialist legal AI tools, potentially for sale to other law firms.
The more usual alternative chosen by many of the firm’s competitors would have been to form partnerships with off-the-shelf AI platforms.
Eltemate has developed proprietary technology for clients, including an AI-powered tool that briefs clients on regulatory changes and an assistant that helps to automate common legal tasks.
the Claude for Legal suite of tools launched in May, following the rollout of legal plug-ins in February.

kp.k: AI-native firms combine technology with retained lawyer judgment
kp.d: Covenant aims to undercut traditional Big Law costs in off-market private investing, operating with five lawyers alongside AI technicians and securing $4mn seed funding in 2025. Norm Law uses agents for initial task assessments reviewed by lawyers, rather than direct unsupervised client reliance. It received $50mn from Blackstone in November 2025 and aspires to become a full-service AI-native firm; neither provider's cost or expansion ambitions are established outcomes here.
qs: Covenant, which aims to offer AI-powered services to clients involved in off-market private investing and to undercut traditional Big Law competitors on cost.
He is part of a small team of five  lawyers at the venture, working alongside AI technicians.
Last year, Covenant secured $4mn in seed funding from Flybridge Capital Partners to accelerate its AI legal services offering.
The model uses AI agents to conduct initial task assessments, which are reviewed by lawyers who advise clients on further action.
The firm secured $50mn from private capital group Blackstone to fund expansion in November 2025.

kp.k: Alternative structures broaden legal service delivery
kp.d: The FT says partnerships remain dominant but describes platform firms, consolidation and shared-infrastructure groups as alternatives. Spain's Ambar connects more than 400 independent lawyers with businesses and envisages supplying some tasks through agents; its matching system uses completed projects and peer references. Lawfront has grown to seven regional firms, while Ampa's house-of-brands model shares infrastructure, technology and development support. These organisational changes are reported alongside AI, not established as caused by it.
qs: The traditional law firm partnership remains the norm.
Based in Spain, Ambar is a service that connects more than 400 independent lawyers with businesses looking for legal services.
It aims to give companies quick and flexible access to legal expertise — whether from lawyers or, for some tasks, AI agents.
The system analyses projects completed by Ambar’s pool of independent lawyers, identifying areas of expertise and drawing on peer references so clients can find the best matches for legal tasks.

Under the “house of brands” model developed by Walker-Smith, the constituent law firms and related service ventures share infrastructure, technology and development support, which offers an alternative to consolidation for regional law firms seeking to scale up.

kp.k: Management services structures facilitate outside investment
kp.d: The report describes management services organisations as a mechanism for receiving outside investment while observing US state restrictions on nonlawyer ownership. Holland & Knight advisers Josh Porte and Trisha Rich work on transaction and ethical frameworks; Rich's 45-lawyer team is handling 100 live transactions. Broadfield, launched in 2024 and backed by Alvarez & Marsal's parent company, aims to offer elite services at mid-market rates with management-services support. This is a parallel ownership and financing development, not an AI-specific regulatory reform.
qs: Porte is an expert in negotiating and executing management services organisation structures that enable law firms to receive outside investment without violating US state laws that typically prohibit non- lawyers from owning firms.
MSOs were developed in the healthcare sector
she directs a team of 45 lawyers who are currently handling 100 live transactions.
Broadfield, launched in 2024, aims to deliver elite legal services at mid-market rates and is backed by the parent company of Alvarez & Marsal, the global turnaround and restructuring consultancy.

kp.k: Data infrastructure and ethical design support legal technology
kp.d: The report identifies supporting capabilities beyond generative tools: Pirical supplies workforce and competitor analytics, including a database exceeding 700,000 legal professionals; Infodash connects existing firm systems and is deployed at more than a quarter of the Am Law 200. Riehl contributes to SALI's legal-data taxonomy, while Fair Patterns aims to identify and replace manipulative AI designs. These are product functions and stated aims, not demonstrated improvements in legal outcomes.
qs: Its products include a database of more than 700,000 legal professionals and a platform to benchmark firms and staff across a range of criteria, including pay.
Infodash is now deployed at more than a quarter of the Am Law 200 ranking of the biggest US law firms by revenue.
Riehl has a leading role at the Sali Alliance, a non-profit initiative to develop a standard taxonomy of legal data
It aims to detect “dark patterns”, or manipulative designs, in AI systems that deceive users, and replace them with safe ones.

kp.k: Political pressure complicates professional independence alongside technological change
kp.d: As a separate pressure on the profession, the FT describes the 2025 executive orders against US firms as forcing a choice between commercial protection and defending professional independence. It reports successful challenges by firms including Jenner & Block, Perkins Coie, WilmerHale and Susman Godfrey while noting continuing administration appeals. This frames legal-sector restructuring within contested professional legitimacy rather than attributing political coercion to AI.
qs: At the same time, the role of commercial lawyers as professionals who are also guardians of the law  and of legal process is being contested.

Law firms targeted by punitive sanctions imposed by US President Donald Trump in 2025 faced a  tough dilemma: capitulate to his demands in order to preserve access to lucrative government  work, or fight back, risking significant financial harm.
Many of the individuals listed here chose the latter course — and have so far been vindicated,  although the administration is appealing against the rulings against it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The FT portrays AI as a potentially fundamental disruption to commercial legal services, enabling automation, in-house substitution for outside counsel, new service models and changes to lawyers’ work and client relationships.
pts.d: The FT’s editorial framing calls AI a potentially existential threat, links it to increased legal-tech investment and the emergence of AI-native firms, and anticipates upheaval in working practices, training and provider–client relationships. Its general-counsel introduction claims that routine work can now be automated and some previously outsourced work performed in-house; more time for senior lawyers to give strategic advice is explicitly presented as a promise, not a measured outcome. Its AI-enablers introduction reports swift adoption and customer-reported time savings and workplace satisfaction, while identifying restructuring client relationships as the next challenge. Specific attributed claims include Eric D. Greenberg’s argument that clients building their own AI-powered legal systems may bypass law firms that do not engage with AI, and Harvey co-founder Gabe Pereyra’s argument that AI will absorb some junior tasks but can also move juniors into higher-value work. The FT reports that Sabastian Niles uses outside counsel’s AI adoption as a retention criterion. It describes Ashurst increasingly organising people and processes around AI and developing billing models reflecting both technology and human skills; Virginia Briggs is planning for possible pricing and remuneration changes. On service delivery, the FT reports that Prosus’s nearly 300 agents offer reductions in labour-intensive tasks; Groenewold-Wong advocates lawyers building their own products with AI. Covenant aims to offer AI-powered private-investment legal services at lower cost than traditional Big Law. Norm Law uses agents for initial task assessments followed by lawyer review and advice, and aspires to become a full-service AI-native firm. Ambar aims to provide flexible access to either lawyers or, for some tasks, agents. The Freshfields–Anthropic partnership could turn a law firm’s specialist tools into products sold to competitors. These accounts combine reported current practices with ambitions and predictions; they do not assert that all legal work can be autonomously substituted.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Support consists principally of interview-based profiles, examples of deployments and organisational changes, investment and adoption figures, customer reports, and named practitioners’ or executives’ arguments—not comparative performance studies.
pts.d: The listing draws on hundreds of interviews conducted by RSGI, followed by research, analysis and peer nominations. This is the stated selection methodology, not a claim-by-claim validation protocol. Legaltech Hub is the named source for the $4.28bn legal-tech investment figure in 2025. Reported deployment examples include more than 100 agents in CrowdStrike’s legal team of over 80 people; nearly 300 agents at Prosus and Groenewold-Wong’s own Claude Code regulatory tracker; a purpose-built platform across Coherent’s legal function that the FT says makes company-wide legal intelligence easier to gather; and a 380-lawyer pilot at Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas before platform selection. Adoption and capital figures include Harvey serving more than 100,000 legal professionals and a March funding valuation of $11bn, and Legora serving clients in more than 50 markets with a $5.6bn valuation after its latest 2026 fundraising. These describe market activity, not demonstrated legal accuracy or productivity. Customer-reported time savings and satisfaction are not accompanied by numerical results, sample sizes or a measurement method. Greenberg’s argument is sourced to his 2025 Bloomberg Law columns; Pereyra’s junior-work prediction is attributed to him without a supporting study. Covenant’s small team of five lawyers working alongside AI technicians and its $4mn seed financing illustrate its model, but the article supplies no comparative cost results. Norm Law’s described workflow and $50mn Blackstone investment illustrate its operations and expansion plans, not verified full-service capability. No model benchmarks, measured error rates, controlled studies, quantified strategic-time gains or employment-displacement estimates are offered for these claims. The source discloses that Harvey and Legora sponsor the FT Live Innovative Lawyers global summit.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes changes already underway by June 2026 from open-ended possibilities for future restructuring; most predictions have no specified completion date.
pts.d: Published on June 26, 2026, the report focuses on work in recent years, especially approximately the preceding 12 months, with interviews from October 2025 through May 2026. Automation, in-house performance of formerly outsourced work, agent deployment, customer-reported gains and some client AI-retention requirements are described as current developments. Greenberg’s account of the changing GC role appeared in 2025. Norm Law’s chair joined in January 2026 after its November 2025 expansion funding; becoming a full-service AI-native firm remains an ambition. Freshfields’ Anthropic deal dates to April 2026 in the report’s context, and selling the resulting tools to rival firms remains a possibility rather than an accomplished outcome. AI’s existential implications, junior lawyers’ move into higher-value work, senior lawyers’ greater strategic capacity, and pricing and remuneration changes are not given a definite horizon. Qualifications matter: Greenberg refers to some in-house teams and specifically to firms failing to engage; Pereyra refers to some junior tasks and says AI can, rather than necessarily will, support higher-value work. Ambar envisages agents only for some tasks. Niles’s agentic-AI advocacy explicitly retains human supervision, and Norm Law’s model retains lawyer review. Training, anxiety management, tracking tool use and responsible adoption are presented as practical requirements for embedding AI, not as quantified guarantees of success.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are commercial law firms, corporate legal departments, junior and senior lawyers, clients and new legal-service entrants; the report does not frame enterprise efficiencies as access-to-justice gains.
pts.d: The report’s main scope is the global commercial legal industry, particularly its elite segment. Managing partners face changes to strategy, service delivery, pricing, remuneration and training. Corporate general counsel and legal departments gain the ability to automate work, build tools and retain work previously sent outside, potentially increasing their strategic role and influence over supplier selection. Niles’s retention criterion makes AI adoption commercially consequential for outside counsel. Junior lawyers may lose some existing tasks while gaining higher-value assignments according to Pereyra; senior lawyers may have more time for business advice, but this is a prospective benefit. Prosus’s product-building example places tool creation within lawyers’ own work. Traditional Big Law faces prospective price competition from Covenant in off-market private investing and client bypass risk in Greenberg’s account. AI-native firms such as Norm Law reorganise service delivery around agents plus lawyers, while Ambar combines independent-lawyer access with the possibility of agents for selected tasks. Harvey and Legora are software-platform vendors, distinct from Factor, which the report identifies as an alternative services provider and describes as offering AI training. Freshfields could additionally supply specialist tools to other firms. The report also describes training and support through the ACC, law schools and firm programmes, affecting lawyers’ skills and professional development. It does not quantify net job losses, forecast a particular staffing shape, or claim that these commercial developments close the civil justice gap.
